blocks.text: [III, 258] VIII. The eighth is ילק jelek, from licking, derived from שילוק בלשונו, because with its tongue it licks the crops and the fruits of the earth. So Aben Ezra on Joel. The Arabs agree with this: for them the verb لحس [laḥasa] lahasa means to lick. And the noun لحس [laḥs] lahas, that is, a licking, is said of the locust, which consumes the produce of the earth by licking it, as the moth does wool. Alcamus: اللحس اكل الدود الصوف واكل [col. 446] الجراد الخضر [al-laḥs akl al-dūd al-ṣūf wa-akl al-jarād al-khuḍar]. Similar is the fact that in Giauhari and Damir العثة [al-ʿuththa], the moth (Hebr. עש), is defined as دويبة تلحس الصوف [duwaybba talḥasu al-ṣūf], a little animal that licks wool, that is, gnaws it. Hence in Scripture to lick sometimes means the same as to consume. So Num. XXII, 4. This multitude will lick up everything that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field. And 1 Reg. XVIII, 20. Then the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering, and the wood, and the stones, and the very dust, and also licked up the water that was in the trench ^{(10)}.

IX. The ninth, סלעם solam, is for Aben Ezra a kind of locust that יעלה בסלעים, climbs the rocks, as though it were formed from סלע with Mem added at the end of the word; but we have already shown that they cite no noun of this form. Not to mention that there is no species of locust more given to rocks than another. We therefore think that in סלעם the final Mem belongs to the root, as in גזם, discussed above ^{a)}. For in Chaldee סלעם means to devour and to consume, like the Hebrew בלע, in place of which it frequently occurs in the Paraphrasts. [III, 259] Hence the locust is rightly called סלעם solam, just as in Greek it is called βροῦχος [brouchos] or βροῦκος [broukos], and ἀκρὶς [akris], on which see below ^{(11)}.

X. The tenth is צלצל tselatsal, Deut. XXVIII, 42. For the Greeks it is ἐρυσίβη [erysibē], for the Vulgate BLIGHT; but for all the Hebrews, for Onkelos and for Erpenianus it is the locust. Many hold that it is so called from the noise of its wings, because צלל means to tinkle, and צלצלים are cymbals or bells. But צלל also means to overshadow. Hence it seems more probable to me that locusts are so called because they overshadow the sun, as we prove in its proper place ^{b)} from Pliny and others. No one observes that the sound of their wings comes close to the ringing of a cymbal or a bell ^{(12)}.
